title: How can many signers share one key?
dek: Everyone in the group must sign. The blockchain receives one ordinary Schnorr signature, with no list of the people who made it.

blocks.text: Several people can share control of a coin without publishing a signature from each person. MuSig2 combines their public keys into one key. When they agree to spend, they exchange messages and combine their contributions into one signature.

Every member of that group must participate. MuSig2 is an n-of-n scheme, not a threshold scheme in which some members can be absent. Its result is an ordinary BIP 340 signature: a verifier checks it just as it would a signature made by one signer.

figure.title: Many participants. One signature.
figure.caption: The group exchanges nonces and partial signatures off chain. A key-path spend reveals the final signature; its public key was already in the output. The published example uses a test message, not a spendable transaction.

blocks.text: Anyone with the full list of public keys can compute the aggregate key. They do not need the signers’ secret keys or an interactive round. But simply adding the public keys is not enough: MuSig2 weights them with coefficients derived from the list.

blocks.title: Not a plain sum
blocks.caption: Three published keys aggregated in two orders, each key weighted by its coefficient, beside what simply adding the keys would give.

blocks.text: Order matters. Reverse the same key list and the aggregate changes. Applications without a natural ordering can use KeySort so everyone starts from the same list.

blocks.summary: The aggregation equation and the coefficient exception

blocks.text: Key aggregation needs no interaction. Given the list of everyone’s public keys, anyone can compute the aggregate: Q = a₁·P₁ + a₂·P₂ + … + aᵤ·Pᵤ. Each coefficient aᵢ is a tagged hash of a hash of the whole key list together with that signer’s own key. The input keys are ordinary 33-byte compressed keys; the output is a 32-byte BIP 340 key.

The coefficients are what make this different from adding keys together: each hashed coefficient depends on the entire list as well as on the key it multiplies. The figure above shows the effect on BIP 327’s own three-key example: the plain sum of the keys matches neither aggregate.

One coefficient is fixed. The second distinct key in the list always gets coefficient 1, an optimization the BIP calls MuSig2*, which saves one point multiplication. The same key may even appear twice; the algorithms handle it, and the BIP recommends omitting duplicate checks to simplify error handling; at that point it is often impossible to tell which signer copied whom. Applications may still reject duplicates, for instance when one owner runs several devices.

The first round exchanges public nonces. Each signer generates a secret nonce and shares its public part, which in MuSig2 is two points rather than one. The public points are aggregated. This round can happen before the message or the final group of signers is known.

Once the message is known, each signer computes the same session values from the aggregate nonce, aggregate key and message. In the second round, each sends a partial signature. The BIP recommends checking one’s own partial signature before sending it.

The partial signatures are added, with an adjustment for any key tweaks. Together with the nonce point’s x coordinate, the sum forms a 64-byte signature checked by an ordinary BIP 340 verifier. The key-path witness contains no participant list.

blocks.title: A signing session, round by round
blocks.caption: The four signature-aggregation vectors published with BIP 327. Follow the public nonces and partial signatures from each signer to the final signature; two examples also apply key tweaks.

blocks.summary: The session equations and the exceptional nonce

blocks.text: Every signer then computes the same session values. A nonce coefficient b is hashed from the aggregate nonce, the aggregate key and the message; the final nonce is R = R₁ + b·R₂, where R₁ and R₂ are the two points of the aggregate nonce; and e is the usual BIP 340 challenge for R, the key and the message. If R₁ + b·R₂ is the point at infinity, which signals a dishonest signer or aggregator, the BIP uses the generator G instead: signing can then continue, and the culprit is caught when partial signatures are verified. One of its signing vectors exercises exactly that case.

In the second round each signer sends a partial signature: a single number, s = k₁ + b·k₂ + e·a·d, built from its two secret nonces, its coefficient and its secret key, with signs adjusted so the final nonce and key have even y. The BIP recommends that a signer verify its own result before sending it.

The aggregate key can be tweaked along the way. A plain tweak derives child keys in the manner of BIP 32; an x-only tweak adds a Taproot commitment, so the same output can be spent either with the group’s signature or through a script path. Two of the vectors in Fig. A14.3 carry tweaks.

MuSig2 has a requirement that single-signer BIP 340 signing does not. The secret nonces must come from a good random generator, and they must not be derived deterministically from the session, because an active adversary could then trick a signer into reusing one.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: Never run Sign twice with the same secret nonce. BIP 327 states that two partial signatures from one nonce make it possible to extract the signer’s secret key.

Two partial signatures made with the same secret nonce can expose the signer’s secret key. BIP 327 allows Sign to erase the secret nonce after reading it, and requires an all-zero nonce to be rejected. The illustrated implementation uses that rule to refuse a second signing attempt.

blocks.title: A nonce is used once
blocks.caption: Schematic, with no values: BIP 327 allows Sign to overwrite the secret nonce with zeros after reading it, and this site’s model does, so a second Sign with that nonce is refused.

blocks.text: NonceGen can also take the secret key, aggregate key and message when they are already known. The BIP recommends these extra inputs as defense in depth against accidental repetition of the random value. They do not replace fresh randomness.

blocks.summary: The exception for one stateless signer

blocks.text: Keeping a secret nonce between rounds is state, and state is where mistakes happen. The BIP allows one exception: a single signer may be stateless, waiting until it has everyone else’s nonces and the full session before generating its own and signing at once, and that signer may sign deterministically. The published deterministic-signing vectors are among those this site’s model reproduces.

blocks.summary: Why two rounds, and why Taproot

blocks.text: The authors list what this costs: MuSig2 cannot generate nonces deterministically, and implementations have to handle signing state securely. Compared with MuSig-DN, they say MuSig2 is substantially less complex; compared with three-round schemes such as MuSig1, it needs only two rounds.

A coin that needs three people to agree can be locked with a script that checks three signatures. That works, but it puts three keys and three signatures on chain, and tells everyone that three people were involved. BIP 327, assigned in 2022 and recorded as deployed, offers another way: a multi-signature scheme called MuSig2, in which the signers combine their keys into one and produce one signature together.

The result is an ordinary BIP 340 key and an ordinary BIP 340 signature. The authors’ primary motivation is letting people using different software jointly control a Taproot output and spend it through its key path; they argue this is more compact, cheaper to verify and more private than an n-of-n script that checks every signer. The standard also supports tweaking the aggregate key, for BIP 32 child keys and for BIP 341 Taproot commitments.

A participant can stop a session by sending a bad contribution. Checking each partial signature helps identify which participant caused the failure. That conclusion depends on the BIP’s conditions: messages must arrive untampered, nonce aggregation must be honest, and every partial signature must be checked.

blocks.title: Checking partial signatures
blocks.caption: BIP 327’s partial-signature cases: a valid one, three that fail the check, and two that point at a bad public nonce or key.

blocks.text: Partial signatures are not signatures in their own right. The BIP points out that an adversary can forge one without the matching secret key; the check exists only to assign blame. If every partial signature passes, their sum is a valid Schnorr signature.

The rounds can also run through an untrusted aggregator that collects and combines everyone’s messages. A malicious aggregator can make the session fail, but cannot forge a signature, even working with all but one of the signers.
MuSig2 produces BIP 340 signatures only. It does not work with ECDSA, and it cannot make progress without every signer whose key contributed to the aggregate.
